presentation: Vaccinated woman invited for cervical screening
stem:
A 25-year-old woman received the HPV vaccine at school when she was 12. She has now received her first invitation for cervical screening and tells her GP she plans to ignore it, because she has been vaccinated and has had only one sexual partner.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Screening is not needed, as the vaccine prevents every case of cervical cancer in vaccinated women
options.B: She can skip screening for as long as she stays with a single partner
options.C: Screening is only needed if she develops bleeding or unusual discharge
options.D: She should attend, as the vaccine does not cover every high-risk type
options.E: She should delay screening until she has had a booster dose of vaccine

correct_answer: D. She should attend, as the vaccine does not cover every high-risk type
why_correct: The HPV vaccine greatly reduces the risk of cervical cancer, but it does not protect against every high-risk HPV type and cannot treat infection already present. Vaccinated women are therefore still invited for cervical screening, which is the way to detect cell changes early. NHS advice is that it remains important to attend screening after vaccination. Source: NHS.uk, HPV vaccine (page last reviewed 1 September 2023).
why_wrong: A. The vaccine reduces cancer risk very substantially but does not prevent every case, so this overstates its protection and would lead to missed screening. B. Risk of HPV exposure is not removed by having one partner, since the partner may carry the virus, and screening eligibility depends on age rather than relationship status. C. Screening is meant for women without symptoms; waiting for bleeding or discharge defeats its purpose of finding changes early. E. There is no booster dose of HPV vaccine to wait for, and screening is not delayed by vaccination status.
pearl: Vaccination lowers the risk of cervical cancer; it does not replace cervical screening.
thinking: Vaccinated at school, now invited for screening  ↓  Vaccine covers the main high-risk HPV types, not all  ↓  Protection is not complete  ↓  Still attend screening
exam_trap: Assuming a vaccinated woman is fully protected and can decline screening.
takeaway: Women vaccinated against HPV should still attend cervical screening when invited.
notes: Re-angled from the bare recall 'main purpose of HPV vaccination' (near-tautological; overlaps live PAQ1149/BX items on the programme) to the practical decision that vaccination does not replace screening; same underlying learning point (vaccine prevents HPV-related cancer but is not complete protection). No live item tests this angle (searched plab1-questions.js).

presentation: Irregular tightenings in late third trimester
stem:
A 31-year-old woman in her second pregnancy, a few weeks before term, telephones the maternity unit because her abdomen keeps tightening in the afternoons. The tightenings come and go, vary in strength, ease when she drinks water and rests, and have not become longer, stronger or closer together. She has had no bleeding or leaking of fluid and the baby is moving normally. In maternity triage her observations are normal, her uterus is soft between tightenings, the cervix is long and closed and the CTG is reassuring.

What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Threatened preterm labour needing admission for tocolysis
options.B: Concealed placental abruption with no visible vaginal bleeding
options.C: Early pre-eclampsia presenting with uterine irritability
options.D: Braxton Hicks (practice) contractions
options.E: An acute urinary tract infection triggering uterine activity

correct_answer: D. Braxton Hicks (practice) contractions
why_correct: Irregular tightenings that do not become more frequent, longer or stronger and are not accompanied by cervical change are typical of Braxton Hicks (practice) contractions. The normal observations, soft uterus between contractions, closed cervix and reassuring CTG argue against labour, abruption or other pathology. She can be reassured and told when to seek help again, for example regular painful contractions, bleeding, fluid loss or reduced movements. Source: NHS.uk, Signs that labour has begun; NICE NG25, Preterm labour and birth, 2015 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: A. True preterm labour needs regular painful contractions that progress with cervical change, and this woman has neither. B. Abruption causes constant pain with a hard, tender uterus and often fetal compromise, whereas her uterus is soft with a normal CTG. C. Pre-eclampsia is suggested by raised blood pressure, proteinuria or severe headache and visual symptoms, and her observations are normal. E. A urinary tract infection may cause some uterine irritability but would be suggested by urinary symptoms or fever, which she does not have.
pearl: Contractions that stay irregular and do not build, with a closed cervix, are Braxton Hicks rather than labour.
thinking: Irregular, non-progressive tightenings  ↓  Normal observations, soft uterus, closed cervix, reassuring CTG  ↓  No bleeding or fluid loss, normal movements  ↓  Braxton Hicks contractions
exam_trap: Admitting every woman with tightenings as threatened preterm labour, or missing real labour by reassuring those whose contractions are building.
takeaway: Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular and do not progress, with no cervical change.
notes: Original was a short recall vignette; rebuilt with normal triage findings so the key is a diagnosis made from absence of progression, not a number. Gestation left as 'a few weeks before term' (no week threshold). Live PAQ16144 tests term latent vs established labour; Braxton Hicks only appears there as a distractor, so not a repeat.

presentation: Pill user with right upper abdominal pain and jaundice
stem:
A 29-year-old woman who has taken a combined oral contraceptive pill for six years has had two days of severe pain in the right upper abdomen. Her partner noticed yesterday that her eyes look yellow, and her urine has become dark. She takes no other medicines, drinks little alcohol and has not travelled. Her temperature is 37.4°C and her blood pressure is normal.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Same-day medical assessment with liver blood tests and abdominal imaging
options.B: Reassure her that these are recognised minor effects of the pill and arrange a routine review next month
options.C: Change to a different brand of combined pill and ask her to report back if the symptoms continue
options.D: Advise simple analgesia and rest, with the symptoms to be reviewed at her next scheduled pill check
options.E: Prescribe a course of oral antibiotics for a presumed urinary tract infection and review in a week

correct_answer: A. Same-day medical assessment with liver blood tests and abdominal imaging
why_correct: Jaundice with severe upper abdominal pain suggests a significant liver or biliary problem and needs prompt assessment with liver function tests and imaging; it should not be put down to the pill. Combined hormonal contraceptives are linked with conditions such as gallbladder disease, Budd-Chiari syndrome and liver tumours, which make them contraindicated or cautioned, so the pill should be reviewed once the cause is clear. NHS advice is that jaundice needs urgent medical assessment. Source: BNF, Ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel (contra-indications and cautions); NHS.uk, Jaundice.
why_wrong: B. Jaundice and severe pain are not minor pill effects; this reassurance would delay diagnosis of serious liver or biliary disease. C. A change of brand does nothing to investigate the cause and exposes her to the same hormones while the diagnosis is unknown. D. Analgesia and a delayed review ignores the red flag of jaundice, which needs investigation now. E. Nothing in the history points to a urinary infection, and antibiotics would not address the likely liver or biliary cause.
pearl: Jaundice in a pill user is a red flag to investigate, not a side effect to accept.
thinking: Pill user with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain  ↓  Dark urine suggests cholestasis or liver disease  ↓  Do not attribute to contraception  ↓  Same-day assessment with liver tests and imaging, then review the pill
exam_trap: Attributing jaundice and severe abdominal pain to the contraceptive pill and reassuring.
takeaway: Jaundice with abdominal pain in a woman on the pill needs same-day assessment, not reassurance.
notes: Source stem was a vague 'what should be considered' item with off-topic distractors; re-angled to a concrete next-step decision. Key is the principle (investigate promptly), not a figure. Not a live duplicate (searched plab1-questions.js for pill + jaundice). Pill-specific wording reflects BNF contra-indications/cautions; CKS page for CHC opened (Last revised in August 2024) but not quoted.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman and her partner have not conceived after 18 months of regular unprotected intercourse. Her periods are unpredictable, coming sometimes after six weeks and sometimes after three months. She is otherwise well with a normal BMI and no pelvic pain, and her partner's semen analysis is normal.

Which blood test is most appropriate to assess the likely cause of her difficulty conceiving?

options.A: Serum FSH and luteinising hormone levels
options.B: Serum CA125 to screen for endometriosis
options.C: Chlamydia antibody testing to assess tubal damage
options.D: Thyroid peroxidase antibody level to look for autoimmunity
options.E: Serum rubella IgG to confirm her immunity status

correct_answer: A. Serum FSH and luteinising hormone levels
why_correct: Irregular cycles point towards an ovulatory disorder, so NICE advises measuring serum gonadotrophins (FSH and LH) in women with irregular cycles who are being investigated for infertility. Further tests such as prolactin are then guided by the clinical picture and results. Source: NICE NG257, Fertility problems: assessment and treatment, 2026.
why_wrong: B. CA125 is not used to diagnose endometriosis, and she has no pelvic pain to suggest it. C. Chlamydia antibodies can help to assess tubal damage, but this does not explain unpredictable cycles. D. Thyroid antibodies are not routine; thyroid function is checked only if she has symptoms of thyroid disease. E. Rubella immunity is a pre-conception check and does not explain a delay in conceiving.
pearl: In a woman with subfertility and irregular cycles, think ovulatory disorder first and check FSH and LH; prolactin is added if an ovulatory disorder, galactorrhoea or pituitary disease is suspected.
thinking: Subfertility with unpredictable cycles  ↓  Semen analysis is normal  ↓  Suspect an ovulatory disorder  ↓  Measure serum FSH and LH
exam_trap: C, chlamydia antibody testing, is a tubal test that tempts as part of a standard subfertility work-up, but her cycle pattern points to ovulation, not tubal damage.
takeaway: Irregular cycles with subfertility call for FSH and LH to assess ovulatory function.
notes: Reframed from the AKT bare-recall item (which keyed 'ovulation' against absurd distractors) into a specific investigation decision. Key matches NG257 rec 1.18.10 (irregular cycles: serum FSH and LH). NG257 (31 March 2026) replaced CG156. No figures keyed. Near-live items differ (DT086/DR105 treatment questions; PAN2375 tubal; PAN3641 prolactinoma).
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg156 (notice that CG156 is replaced by NG257)

stem:
A 31-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has had no flare for more than a year on hydroxychloroquine and mycophenolate mofetil. She and her partner would like to start a family and she asks her GP how to go about it.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Stop all lupus medicines now, including hydroxychloroquine, so the baby is never exposed
options.B: Try to conceive straight away and review her medicines once the pregnancy is confirmed
options.C: Arrange a planned pre-pregnancy review so unsafe medicines can be switched safely
options.D: Continue every current medicine unchanged because disease control matters most
options.E: Advise that pregnancy is unsafe in lupus and she should not try to conceive

correct_answer: C. Arrange a planned pre-pregnancy review so unsafe medicines can be switched safely
why_correct: Pregnancy is best planned when lupus is quiet, and some medicines, including mycophenolate, are harmful in pregnancy and must be changed before conception, whereas hydroxychloroquine is usually continued. A planned review with the rheumatology team allows medicines to be adjusted and specialist antenatal care to be arranged. Source: NHS.uk, Lupus (advice to see a doctor before trying to get pregnant so medicines can be checked); British Society for Rheumatology prescribing-in-pregnancy guidance (taught standard, full text not opened).
why_wrong: A. Stopping hydroxychloroquine risks a flare, which is itself harmful to mother and baby. B. Medicines must be changed before conception because mycophenolate can harm the fetus in early pregnancy. D. Some medicines, such as mycophenolate, are teratogenic and cannot simply be continued. E. Most women with well-controlled lupus can have a successful pregnancy, so pregnancy is not absolutely contraindicated.
pearl: In SLE, plan pregnancy for a time of quiet disease, switch teratogenic drugs such as mycophenolate beforehand, usually continue hydroxychloroquine and arrange specialist-led care.
thinking: SLE and planning pregnancy  ↓  Disease quiet but on mycophenolate  ↓  Teratogenic drug needs changing, hydroxychloroquine usually continued  ↓  Planned pre-pregnancy rheumatology review
exam_trap: A, stopping everything, sounds cautious but removes hydroxychloroquine, which protects against flares and is usually continued.
takeaway: Plan pregnancy in SLE with a pre-pregnancy medicines review rather than stopping all treatment or waiting for a positive test.
notes: AKT source distractor 'stop hydroxychloroquine' was the wrong direction and key was generic; reframed with a named teratogen (mycophenolate) to make the decision real. No national guideline page for SLE pregnancy could be fetched (CKS lupus 404; BSR page was a listing only; Lupus UK 404): only NHS.uk Lupus opened, so the BSR statement is standard teaching and is flagged as not opened in why_correct. Reviewer may wish to confirm against BSR 2016/2017 prescribing-in-pregnancy guideline. No live duplicate (DT158 contraception, PAQ16479 APS pregnancy).

presentation: Lower abdominal pain, woman of reproductive age
stem:
A 24-year-old woman attends the emergency department with 10 hours of lower abdominal pain, mild nausea and tenderness in the right iliac fossa. She is afebrile and haemodynamically stable, her periods are regular and her last period ended a week ago, and she uses condoms most of the time.

Which investigation should be done as part of the initial assessment before any imaging is requested?

options.A: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis
options.B: Serum CA125 measurement
options.C: Urinalysis for microscopic haematuria
options.D: Urine pregnancy test
options.E: Plain abdominal radiograph

correct_answer: D. Urine pregnancy test
why_correct: Pregnancy status changes the differential diagnosis, since ectopic pregnancy can resemble gastrointestinal or urinary causes of pain, and it influences imaging, prescribing and surgical decisions. NICE advises being aware that women of reproductive age may be pregnant and offering a pregnancy test even when symptoms are non-specific. Source: NICE NG126, Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management, 2019 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. CT uses ionising radiation, so pregnancy must be excluded first and it is not the first step. B. CA125 is not a test for acute abdominal pain and is not used as an initial investigation. C. Urinalysis is useful but would not exclude pregnancy, which is the key safety check. E. A plain radiograph exposes the pelvis to radiation and rarely helps in this setting.
pearl: Think of pregnancy in every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, even when the history seems to make it unlikely; the result changes the differential, imaging and drug choices.
thinking: Woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain  ↓  Pregnancy cannot be excluded by history alone  ↓  Test before imaging or surgery  ↓  Urine pregnancy test
exam_trap: A, CT scan, is attractive when appendicitis is suspected, but it should not be done before pregnancy is excluded.
takeaway: Do a pregnancy test in all women of reproductive age with abdominal pain, whatever the history.
notes: Rewritten from the AKT why-is-pregnancy-testing-important item to a concrete action; stem deliberately gives regular periods and condom use so the stem does not cue the answer. Key follows NG126 rec 1.4.5. Live OG043/PAQ16583/PAQ1238 test known ectopic; no live item covers routine testing before imaging.

stem:
A 25-year-old woman in her second pregnancy attends maternity triage at 31 weeks with three hours of painful tightenings every few minutes that are becoming stronger. Her membranes are intact and there is no vaginal bleeding. Her cervix is dilated on examination and has dilated further when the midwife re-examines her an hour later.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Braxton Hicks contractions without cervical change
options.B: Placental abruption with concealed bleeding
options.C: Preterm prelabour rupture of the membranes
options.D: Acute pyelonephritis causing uterine irritability
options.E: Established preterm labour needing urgent care

correct_answer: E. Established preterm labour needing urgent care
why_correct: Regular, increasingly strong contractions with progressive cervical dilatation before term indicate established preterm labour. NICE defines this by progressive dilatation with regular contractions, and it triggers transfer, antenatal corticosteroids and neuroprotection decisions. Source: NICE NG25, Preterm labour and birth, 2015 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: A. Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular and cause no progressive cervical change. B. Abruption usually causes constant pain, a hard uterus or bleeding, which are absent here. C. The membranes are stated to be intact, so rupture has not occurred. D. Pyelonephritis would cause fever and loin pain, and would not produce progressive cervical dilatation.
pearl: Regular contractions with progressive cervical dilatation before term mean established preterm labour; the next steps are steroids, transfer to a unit with neonatal cover and magnesium sulfate at earlier gestations.
thinking: Painful contractions before term  ↓  Cervix dilating on repeat examination  ↓  Not Braxton Hicks, abruption or ruptured membranes  ↓  Established preterm labour needing urgent care
exam_trap: A, Braxton Hicks contractions, is tempting for painful tightenings in pregnancy, but they do not change the cervix.
takeaway: Contractions with progressive cervical dilatation before term are established preterm labour.
notes: Re-angled from a recall definition (key restated the stem) into a differential-diagnosis vignette; the cervical-dilatation figure and the 37-week threshold are not keyed. Live PAOG027/OG055/DS135 test management of preterm labour, not the diagnosis. NG25 page lists the definition of established preterm labour (progressive dilatation from 4 cm with regular contractions), deliberately not quoted as a figure.

stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 14 weeks of pregnancy has had two days of dysuria, urinary frequency and suprapubic discomfort. She is afebrile with no loin pain or vomiting, and urine dipstick shows leucocytes and nitrites.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Send urine for culture and start a safe antibiotic now
options.B: Advise fluids and paracetamol, treating only if a fever develops
options.C: Delay any antibiotic until the culture result is available
options.D: Start a broad-spectrum antibiotic without sending a urine sample
options.E: Arrange urgent hospital admission for intravenous antibiotics

correct_answer: A. Send urine for culture and start a safe antibiotic now
why_correct: Lower urinary tract infection in pregnancy is treated promptly because untreated infection can progress to pyelonephritis. NICE advises an immediate antibiotic prescription, sending a midstream urine sample for culture before antibiotics are taken, and reviewing the antibiotic when susceptibility results are available. Source: NICE NG109, Urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing, 2018.
why_wrong: B. Watchful waiting is not appropriate in pregnancy because infection can ascend to the kidneys. C. Delaying treatment leaves her at risk of pyelonephritis; she should be treated immediately and the antibiotic reviewed against the culture. D. A urine sample for culture must be sent before antibiotics so that treatment can be reviewed against susceptibilities. E. She is systemically well with no features of pyelonephritis, so oral treatment in the community is appropriate.
pearl: In pregnancy, treat lower UTI at once after sending a midstream urine culture, choose a pregnancy-safe antibiotic, and review it when the susceptibilities return.
thinking: Dysuria in pregnancy  ↓  No fever or loin pain, so lower UTI  ↓  Treat promptly because of risk of pyelonephritis  ↓  Send culture and start safe antibiotic
exam_trap: C, waiting for culture, copies the non-pregnant back-up-prescription approach, which does not apply in pregnancy.
takeaway: Pregnant women with lower UTI need a culture sent and immediate antibiotic treatment.
notes: AKT key was a bare diagnosis recall; re-angled to a management decision matching NG109 rec 1.1.5 to 1.1.7. No specific antibiotic or dose keyed (movable and trimester-dependent). Live PAQ14935 covers asymptomatic bacteriuria and DS145 pyelonephritis, not symptomatic lower UTI. NG109 first published 31 Oct 2018; no last-updated date shown on the page.

presentation: Severe period pain in an adolescent
stem:
A 16-year-old girl has had cramping pelvic pain with every period since she was 13, and it has worsened each year. She now misses school for two or three days each month, and ibuprofen and paracetamol only partly help. She is not sexually active, and her abdominal examination is normal.

Which diagnosis should be considered?

options.A: Pelvic inflammatory disease from untreated infection
options.B: Endometriosis causing cyclical period-related pain
options.C: Acute appendicitis with localised peritonism
options.D: Recurrent urinary tract infection of the bladder
options.E: Irritable bowel syndrome with cyclical symptoms

correct_answer: B. Endometriosis causing cyclical period-related pain
why_correct: NICE advises suspecting endometriosis in young women, including those aged 17 and under, with period-related pain that affects daily activities. Progressive pain, missed school and a partial response to simple analgesia fit this, and referral to paediatric and adolescent gynaecology is advised for assessment. Source: NICE NG73, Endometriosis: diagnosis and management, 2017 (updated 2024).
why_wrong: A. Pelvic inflammatory disease needs sexual exposure and typically causes discharge, fever or intermenstrual pain. C. Appendicitis causes acute migratory pain with fever, not recurring pain tied to every period for years. D. A urinary infection would cause urinary symptoms rather than pain that follows her menstrual cycle. E. Irritable bowel syndrome causes bowel-related pain with altered habit, not pain tied to menstruation.
pearl: Suspect endometriosis in adolescents whose period pain is severe, progressive and disrupts school or daily life, to avoid long diagnostic delay.
thinking: Period pain since menarche, worsening  ↓  Missing school with poor response to analgesia  ↓  Persistent and impairing  ↓  Consider endometriosis
exam_trap: Dismissing adolescent period pain as normal delays diagnosis; routine examination is often normal in endometriosis.
takeaway: Severe, progressive period pain affecting daily life in a teenager should prompt consideration of endometriosis.
notes: AKT stem listed obviously wrong distractors; re-angled to progressive pain with partial analgesic response. Live PAQ922 (15-year-old, primary dysmenorrhoea, key NSAID) is the contrasting picture (static pain, regular flow); learning point differs (diagnosis of endometriosis vs first-line treatment). Reviewer to note borderline similarity of setting.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with regular 28-day cycles, no current hormonal contraception and a negative pregnancy test wants to start a combined oral contraceptive pill today, which is day 12 of her cycle. She asks whether she will be protected straight away.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: She is protected immediately, because the pill works from the first tablet
options.B: She needs no extra protection if she takes the pill at the same time each day
options.C: She should use condoms or avoid sex for the first full week of taking the pill
options.D: She must wait until her next period to start because starting mid-cycle is unsafe
options.E: She should take two tablets daily in the first week to gain rapid protection

correct_answer: C. She should use condoms or avoid sex for the first full week of taking the pill
why_correct: The cycle day on which the pill is started determines whether protection is immediate. Starting in the first few days of the cycle gives immediate cover, but starting at any other time, provided pregnancy is reasonably excluded, needs additional contraception for the first week. Source: NICE CKS, Contraception - combined hormonal methods, Last revised in August 2024.
why_wrong: A. Immediate protection applies only when the pill is started in the first days of the cycle, which is not the case here. B. Regular timing helps efficacy but does not give cover before ovulation is suppressed. D. The pill can be started at any point in the cycle if pregnancy is reasonably excluded. E. Doubling the dose is unsafe, adds side effects and does not speed up protection.
pearl: Starting the combined pill early in the cycle gives immediate cover; starting later needs extra contraception such as condoms for the first week.
thinking: Start combined pill mid-cycle  ↓  Pregnancy reasonably excluded  ↓  Outside early cycle days, ovulation not yet suppressed  ↓  Extra contraception for the first week
exam_trap: A, immediate protection, is the common assumption, but it holds only for starts in the first days of the cycle.
takeaway: A mid-cycle start of the combined pill needs additional contraception for the first week.
notes: AKT item keyed cycle day in a factor-recall format; re-angled to the advice decision. The first-few-days window and 7-day figure are expressed in words (first week) rather than keyed numerically. CKS COC page also lists the Qlaira/Zoely exceptions (9 days), omitted for simplicity; stem uses a standard pill. Live ID037/BX282/PAN6001 cover missed pills, not starting.

stem:
A 24-year-old non-smoker with a normal BMI is about to start a combined oral contraceptive pill. During counselling the nurse explains that the oestrogen component is linked to one uncommon but serious adverse effect that she should be told about.

Which adverse effect is this?

options.A: Blood clots in the deep veins of the legs or the lungs
options.B: Permanent reduction in fertility after stopping the pill
options.C: A higher lifetime chance of developing ovarian cancer
options.D: Loss of bone density leading to early osteoporosis
options.E: Progressive scarring of the liver with long-term use

correct_answer: A. Blood clots in the deep veins of the legs or the lungs
why_correct: Oestrogen-containing combined hormonal contraception increases the risk of venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism), even in healthy young women. The absolute risk is small, but it is the key serious adverse effect to explain, and she should be told to seek urgent help for unilateral calf swelling or sudden breathlessness. Source: NHS, Combined pill (patient information); BNF treatment summary, Contraceptives, hormonal.
why_wrong: B. Fertility returns promptly after stopping the pill; it does not cause permanent subfertility. C. Combined pill use is associated with a lower, not higher, risk of ovarian cancer. D. Loss of bone density is a concern with depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, not the combined pill. E. The combined pill does not cause progressive liver scarring.
pearl: Oestrogen in combined hormonal contraception raises the risk of venous thromboembolism, which is why personal and family history of clots is checked before prescribing.
thinking: Combined pill contains oestrogen  ↓  Oestrogen promotes clotting  ↓  Serious adverse effect is venous thromboembolism  ↓  Counsel on calf swelling and sudden breathlessness
exam_trap: Choosing ovarian cancer: the combined pill reduces ovarian cancer risk, so the direction of the association is the trap.
takeaway: The combined pill increases venous thromboembolism risk, so ask about clots in the personal and family history before prescribing.
notes: Re-angled from a bare adverse-effect recall item into a counselling vignette (healthy 24-year-old). Learning point unchanged; no figures. The NHS combined-pill page opened only lists past blood clots in its suitability text, and the BNF treatment summary only mentions CHC with thromboprophylaxis; the VTE link itself is standard teaching (the CKS combined hormonal methods page rendered without readable content, so it is not cited). Reviewer: confirm citation wording acceptable. No live duplicate found (live items cover CHC contraindications, migraine with aura and pill vomiting, not general VTE counselling).

stem:
A 27-year-old woman at 18 weeks of pregnancy attends her GP with three days of dysuria and urinary frequency. She has no fever, loin pain or vomiting and her observations are normal. A urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leucocytes.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Send a urine sample for culture and start an antibiotic
options.B: Advise fluids and cranberry juice, then review if no better
options.C: Withhold antibiotics until the culture result is available
options.D: Prescribe an antibiotic without sending a urine sample
options.E: Reassure her that mild symptoms need no treatment now

correct_answer: A. Send a urine sample for culture and start an antibiotic
why_correct: Lower urinary tract infection in pregnancy should be treated because infection can ascend to the kidneys and cause pyelonephritis, which is associated with complications for mother and baby. NICE advises obtaining a midstream urine sample for culture before antibiotics and offering an immediate antibiotic prescription, then reviewing the choice when the result is back. Source: NICE NG109, Urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing, 2018.
why_wrong: B. Fluids and cranberry juice are not an adequate treatment for a probable infection in pregnancy. C. Delaying antibiotics until the culture is back risks progression to pyelonephritis; treatment is started immediately and reviewed against sensitivities. D. Antibiotics without a culture sample leave no way to review the choice if she does not improve or the organism is resistant. E. Symptomatic urinary infection in pregnancy always needs treatment, however mild.
pearl: In pregnancy a urinary infection is treated promptly, with a culture sample taken first, because it can progress to pyelonephritis.
thinking: Pregnant woman with lower urinary tract symptoms  ↓  Dipstick suggests infection  ↓  Risk of ascending infection to the kidneys  ↓  Culture sample first, then immediate antibiotic
exam_trap: Waiting for the culture result before treating: this can be reasonable in some non-pregnant women, but pregnancy lowers the threshold to treat now.
takeaway: Send a urine culture and start an antibiotic straight away for lower urinary tract infection in pregnancy.
notes: Original AKT item asked why UTI matters (progression to pyelonephritis); re-angled into a management decision with the same principle. No drug or dose is keyed. Distinct from live PAQ14935 (asymptomatic bacteriuria) and DS145 (pyelonephritis, cefalexin), which test different decisions. NG109 recs 1.1.5 and 1.1.6 verified on the opened page.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman has been trying to conceive for 14 months. Her periods come every 6 to 10 weeks, she has a BMI of 34 kg/m² and she has mild facial acne. Her partner's semen analysis is normal.

Which mechanism most likely explains her difficulty conceiving?

options.A: Rare or absent release of eggs from the ovaries
options.B: Blockage of both fallopian tubes by pelvic scarring
options.C: Fibroids distorting the cavity of the uterus
options.D: Antisperm antibodies within the cervical mucus
options.E: Endometriosis involving both of her ovaries

correct_answer: A. Rare or absent release of eggs from the ovaries
why_correct: Very irregular cycles in a woman who is struggling to conceive point to infrequent or absent ovulation, because eggs are released only occasionally. Ovulatory disorders are a leading cause of infertility, and initial work-up includes confirming ovulation with a mid-luteal phase progesterone and checking gonadotrophins when cycles are irregular. Source: NICE CKS, Infertility, Last revised in July 2023.
why_wrong: B. Tubal blockage usually follows pelvic infection or surgery and does not itself disturb cycle length. C. Fibroids distorting the cavity may cause heavy bleeding or miscarriage, not cycles that are weeks apart. D. Antisperm antibodies are an uncommon cause and are not suggested by irregular cycles. E. Endometriosis typically causes cyclical pain and painful sex rather than markedly irregular cycles.
pearl: Irregular or absent periods in a woman with subfertility usually mean ovulation is infrequent or not happening.
thinking: Trying to conceive for over a year  ↓  Normal semen analysis  ↓  Very irregular cycles suggest ovulatory dysfunction  ↓  Infrequent or absent ovulation
exam_trap: Choosing tubal blockage: tubal damage is a common cause overall, but nothing in this history points to it and cycles would remain regular.
takeaway: Markedly irregular cycles with subfertility suggest an ovulatory disorder.
notes: Original was a bare recall item with obviously unrelated distractors (ear, cornea, bone); built a vignette with plausible reproductive distractors. No figures are keyed (14 months and BMI are context only). CKS states ovulatory disorders are a leading cause of infertility. Distinct from live OG030 (PMOS diagnostic criteria) and PAN2375 (tubal factor). The vignette resembles PMOS but the question tests the ovulation mechanism, not the diagnosis.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman has a positive home pregnancy test after six weeks of amenorrhoea. She has no pain or bleeding. Her history includes one uncomplicated term vaginal birth, iron-deficiency anaemia treated with oral iron last year, and emergency surgery three years ago to remove a pregnancy that had implanted in her left fallopian tube.

Which feature of her history most increases the risk that this pregnancy is also ectopic?

options.A: Iron-deficiency anaemia treated with oral iron last year
options.B: A previous ectopic pregnancy treated surgically
options.C: One uncomplicated term vaginal birth four years ago
options.D: Regular moderate exercise since her teenage years
options.E: Lifelong lactose intolerance managed with dietary changes

correct_answer: B. A previous ectopic pregnancy treated surgically
why_correct: A previous ectopic pregnancy is one of the strongest risk factors for another, reflecting underlying tubal damage that impairs transport of the embryo to the uterus. Other recognised factors include pelvic inflammatory disease, previous pelvic or tubal surgery and smoking, so she needs an early assessment to locate the pregnancy even though she has no symptoms yet. Source: NICE CKS, Ectopic pregnancy, Last revised in June 2026.
why_wrong: A. Iron-deficiency anaemia is not a recognised risk factor for ectopic pregnancy. C. An uncomplicated term vaginal birth does not damage the fallopian tubes and is not a specific risk factor. D. Regular exercise is not associated with ectopic pregnancy. E. Lactose intolerance has no link with tubal function or implantation.
pearl: A previous ectopic pregnancy carries a markedly raised chance of recurrence, so such women need early pregnancy assessment.
thinking: Positive pregnancy test with a past tubal pregnancy  ↓  Tubal damage impairs embryo transport  ↓  Recurrence risk is raised  ↓  Previous ectopic pregnancy is the main risk factor
exam_trap: Picking the uncomplicated birth: a normal pregnancy history is reassuring, not a risk factor.
takeaway: Previous ectopic pregnancy is a leading risk factor for another, so locate the pregnancy early.
notes: Original was a bare recall item (which factor increases ectopic risk); wrapped it in a vignette. The stem necessarily states the past ectopic because the question asks to select it among history features. Recurrence percentages deliberately not used. Distinct from live ectopic items (OG014, OG040, OG043, PAOG005, PAOG013, PAQ16583, PAAKT137), which test diagnosis and management, not risk factors. Key is the shortest option.

stem:
A 48-year-old woman with a BMI of 39 kg/m² and long-standing infrequent ovulation has had several months of irregular, heavy vaginal bleeding. An endometrial biopsy shows atypical endometrial hyperplasia, and the gynaecologist explains that this result needs active management.

Why does this finding matter?

options.A: It shows that cervical cancer has already developed
options.B: It can progress to womb lining cancer if left untreated
options.C: It is a harmless oestrogen effect that needs no follow-up
options.D: It is the usual cause of fibroid growth within the uterus
options.E: It means that pelvic inflammatory disease is very likely

correct_answer: B. It can progress to womb lining cancer if left untreated
why_correct: Endometrial hyperplasia, especially with atypia, is a precursor of endometrial cancer and can progress to it if left untreated. It is driven by prolonged oestrogen exposure without enough progestogen, as occurs with obesity and anovulatory cycles, so management (progestogen therapy or hysterectomy) is individualised under gynaecology. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 67, Management of Endometrial Hyperplasia, 2016.
why_wrong: A. Endometrial hyperplasia arises in the womb lining and is unrelated to the cervix. C. Atypical hyperplasia is not harmless; it needs treatment and follow-up because of malignant potential. D. Fibroid growth is a separate, oestrogen-sensitive process and hyperplasia does not cause it. E. Hyperplasia is a hormonal change, not an infective one, and does not indicate pelvic infection.
pearl: Endometrial hyperplasia, particularly atypical hyperplasia, is the recognised precursor of endometrial cancer.
thinking: Prolonged unopposed oestrogen exposure  ↓  Abnormal bleeding and biopsy shows atypical hyperplasia  ↓  Premalignant change of the endometrium  ↓  Risk of progression to endometrial cancer
exam_trap: Dismissing hyperplasia as a benign hormonal effect: without atypia the risk is lower, but it still needs assessment and treatment decisions.
takeaway: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia can progress to endometrial cancer, so it needs active management.
notes: Source asked which condition can precede endometrial cancer; reversed to a vignette asking why the biopsy finding matters (same learning point). Source key was sound. No percentages used. Live OG027 (risk factors), BX284 and DS141 (progestogen protection) test different points; no live item asks about the premalignant nature of hyperplasia. RCOG page opened states hyperplasia is the precursor of endometrial cancer and can progress if untreated; page shows last reviewed 26 February 2016. Management wording (progestogen or hysterectomy) is supported by the NHS postmenopausal bleeding page opened.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman in her first pregnancy has been taking a standard daily folic acid supplement since before she conceived. At her midwife appointment she says she has read that the baby's spine has already formed, so she wonders whether she can stop. She has no personal or family history of neural tube defects, takes no regular medication and does not have diabetes.

What advice should she be given?

options.A: Stop now, because the neural tube has already closed
options.B: Move to a higher prescribed dose until the birth
options.C: Replace it with a vitamin B12 supplement for the rest of pregnancy
options.D: Continue the standard dose until the end of the first trimester
options.E: Stop once the mid-pregnancy anomaly scan has been completed

correct_answer: D. Continue the standard dose until the end of the first trimester
why_correct: Women without added risk factors are advised to take a standard folic acid supplement before conception and through the first trimester of pregnancy to reduce the risk of neural tube defects. She should therefore continue until the end of that period rather than stop early. Higher-dose folic acid is reserved for women at increased risk. Source: NHS.uk, About folic acid; NICE CKS antenatal care confirms advice on folic acid should be given from first contact.
why_wrong: A. Although the neural tube closes early, the standard advice is to continue through the first trimester. B. A higher dose is prescribed only for women with risk factors such as a previous affected pregnancy, diabetes or certain anti-seizure medicines. C. Vitamin B12 is not a substitute for folic acid in preventing neural tube defects. E. There is no link between the anomaly scan and when to stop folic acid.
pearl: Standard-dose folic acid continues to the end of the first trimester; higher doses are for women with defined risk factors.
thinking: Pregnant, standard-risk, on folic acid  ↓  Neural tube forms early but advice still covers first trimester  ↓  No risk factors, so no higher dose  ↓  Continue standard dose to end of first trimester
exam_trap: A seems logical because closure happens early, but guidance still covers the whole first trimester.
takeaway: Continue standard-dose folic acid to the end of the first trimester unless risk factors call for more.
notes: Key is a time window in words (end of first trimester), not a number; the principle (continue, do not stop early or switch) is the point, and the numeric dose/duration is not tested. The NHS page says to take it for the first 12 weeks; CKS antenatal page (Last revised in October 2025) confirms folic acid advice from first contact but gives no dose detail. No live PLAB 1 item tests antenatal folic acid advice (HAE031 is treatment of folate deficiency anaemia).

stem:
A 29-year-old woman attends the emergency department with sudden, severe right-sided pelvic pain that began during sex the previous evening. A urine pregnancy test is negative. She is afebrile, and her pulse and blood pressure are normal. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a small volume of free pelvic fluid and a collapsed cyst on the right ovary, which has a normal size and preserved blood flow.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Ruptured functional ovarian cyst with minor bleeding
options.B: Ovarian torsion with loss of the ovarian blood supply
options.C: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with intraperitoneal bleeding
options.D: Perforated appendicitis with localised peritonitis
options.E: Tubo-ovarian abscess secondary to pelvic infection

correct_answer: A. Ruptured functional ovarian cyst with minor bleeding
why_correct: Sudden unilateral pelvic pain after sex or exertion, a negative pregnancy test, free fluid and a collapsed cyst on an ovary with preserved blood flow identify a ruptured ovarian cyst. Stable patients are usually managed with analgesia and observation, with surgery reserved for ongoing bleeding or instability. Source: NHS.uk, Ovarian cyst (symptoms include sudden severe pain if a cyst splits).
why_wrong: B. Torsion causes pain with vomiting and an enlarged ovary with reduced Doppler flow, which are absent here. C. A negative pregnancy test effectively excludes an ectopic pregnancy. D. Appendicitis would give fever and migratory pain, and would not explain a collapsed ovarian cyst. E. A tubo-ovarian abscess would cause fever, raised inflammatory markers and a complex adnexal mass rather than a collapsed simple cyst.
pearl: Free fluid with a collapsed cyst after a sudden onset of pain points to rupture; check Doppler flow to avoid missing torsion.
thinking: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain  ↓  Pregnancy test negative, so ectopic unlikely  ↓  Collapsed cyst, free fluid, normal ovary and flow  ↓  Ruptured ovarian cyst
exam_trap: B, ovarian torsion, is the dangerous mimic, but preserved Doppler flow and a normal-sized ovary argue against it.
takeaway: A collapsed cyst with free fluid and a negative pregnancy test means a ruptured ovarian cyst.
notes: Diagnosis-only item re-angled with a new vignette (post-coital onset, normal Doppler as the discriminator from torsion); no live PLAB 1 item has ruptured cyst as the answer (BX095/OG037 are torsion). Source key is sound. NHS page confirms rupture causes sudden severe pain and pain during sex; stable-patient conservative management is standard teaching (RCOG/NICE page not opened for this).

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with a history of deep vein thrombosis after a long-haul flight asks her practice nurse about long-acting contraception. The nurse suggests the implant placed under the skin of the upper arm. She asks which hormone it releases and whether it contains oestrogen.

Which statement about the hormone in the contraceptive implant most commonly used in the UK is correct?

options.A: Ethinylestradiol combined with a progestogen, released in a low continuous dose
options.B: Oestradiol alone, released slowly from the rod to suppress ovulation
options.C: Etonogestrel, a progestogen released alone, with no oestrogen component
options.D: Medroxyprogesterone acetate, released slowly from the rod under the skin
options.E: Copper ions, which act locally to prevent fertilisation at the implant site

correct_answer: C. Etonogestrel, a progestogen released alone, with no oestrogen component
why_correct: The implant widely used in the UK releases etonogestrel, a progestogen, and contains no oestrogen. This is why it is a progestogen-only method that can be considered when oestrogen is best avoided, although her history still needs a proper contraceptive assessment. Source: BNF, Etonogestrel (subdermal implant), accessed October 2026.
why_wrong: A. Combined hormonal methods contain ethinylestradiol, but the implant does not. B. No contraceptive implant releases oestradiol alone. D. Medroxyprogesterone acetate is the progestogen in the injectable, not the implant. E. Copper is the mechanism of the copper intrauterine device and is not a subdermal method.
pearl: The arm implant is a progestogen-only method (etonogestrel); the injectable is medroxyprogesterone and the coil is copper or levonorgestrel.
thinking: Implant in the upper arm  ↓  Subdermal rod releases a single hormone  ↓  Progestogen only, no oestrogen  ↓  Etonogestrel
exam_trap: A is tempting because oestrogen is the usual hormone people associate with contraception, but combined methods are a different class.
takeaway: The UK contraceptive implant releases etonogestrel, a progestogen with no oestrogen.
notes: Bare recall item rebuilt as a short vignette around the same fact (a history of VTE makes the oestrogen-free point relevant). I deliberately avoided stating a UKMEC category or duration of use (movable figures) and did not fetch FSRH; BNF page confirms etonogestrel subdermal implant. No live item tests the hormone content of the implant (BX502 tests only that it is LARC).

stem:
A 31-year-old woman with irregular cycles has a positive pregnancy test at her GP surgery. She cannot recall the date of her last period. The midwife needs a reliable estimate of gestational age so that screening and antenatal care can be planned correctly.

Which is the most appropriate way to establish how far advanced the pregnancy is?

options.A: Ultrasound measurement of the fetus
options.B: Symphysis-fundal height measured at the booking visit
options.C: Serum progesterone concentration taken that day
options.D: Quantitative urinary hCG concentration at the surgery
options.E: Maternal weight gain compared with her pre-pregnancy weight

correct_answer: A. Ultrasound measurement of the fetus
why_correct: When the last menstrual period is unknown or cycles are irregular, gestational age is best established by ultrasound measurement of the embryo or fetus. NICE antenatal care recommends an early scan to determine gestational age, which also guides the timing of screening tests. Source: NICE NG201, Antenatal care, 2021.
why_wrong: B. Symphysis-fundal height is a later growth assessment and is not accurate for dating in early pregnancy. C. Progesterone levels vary widely and cannot give a gestational age. D. hCG concentration varies too much between women to date a pregnancy. E. Weight gain is non-specific and unrelated to gestational age.
pearl: Biochemical tests confirm pregnancy but only ultrasound measurement dates it when the last period is uncertain.
thinking: Positive test, last period unknown  ↓  Hormone levels vary between women  ↓  Biometry on ultrasound gives a reliable estimate  ↓  Ultrasound dating
exam_trap: C and D tempt because hormone levels rise in pregnancy, but they confirm pregnancy rather than date it.
takeaway: Date a pregnancy with uncertain last period by ultrasound.
notes: Re-angled with a new vignette (irregular cycles). No numeric gestation keyed; source key sound. NG201 1.2.14 states the early scan determines gestational age; CKS antenatal care (Last revised in October 2025) also describes the dating scan. No live duplicate found (searched 'dating', 'menstrual period').

stem:
A 27-year-old woman is visited by the community midwife six days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. She feels well and has no fever. She describes red-brown vaginal loss that is lighter than in the first days, with no clots and no offensive smell. Her uterus is not tender and is getting smaller, and she is eating, drinking and passing urine normally.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Arrange same-day vaginal swabs and start empirical antibiotics for suspected endometritis
options.B: Refer her urgently for an ultrasound scan to look for retained placental tissue
options.C: Reassure her that this is normal lochia, and explain which warning signs need review
options.D: Prescribe tranexamic acid to reduce the loss and arrange review next week
options.E: Admit her to the maternity unit for assessment of secondary postpartum haemorrhage

correct_answer: C. Reassure her that this is normal lochia, and explain which warning signs need review
why_correct: Lochia is the normal vaginal discharge after birth, starting red and gradually becoming lighter and then pale over the following weeks. With no fever, offensive smell, clots, uterine tenderness or heavy bleeding, reassurance is appropriate. NICE advises explaining what bleeding to expect and to seek advice if it is sudden or very heavy, increases, contains clots or tissue, or comes with signs of infection. Source: NICE NG194, Postnatal care, 2021.
why_wrong: A. Endometritis would cause fever, tender uterus and offensive loss, none of which she has. B. Retained tissue would cause persistent or increasing bleeding and a bulky uterus. D. Tranexamic acid is not needed for expected, settling lochia. E. Secondary postpartum haemorrhage involves heavy or increasing bleeding, which is not described.
pearl: Lochia is expected after every birth; worry about bleeding that is sudden, heavy, increasing, clotty or offensive, or accompanied by fever or pain.
thinking: Postnatal day six, well, afebrile  ↓  Loss lighter, red-brown, no smell, no clots  ↓  Uterus involuting, non-tender  ↓  Normal lochia: reassure and safety-net
exam_trap: A and E over-treat normal lochia; the red flags are fever, offensive loss, tenderness, clots or heavy and increasing bleeding.
takeaway: Normal lochia settles gradually and needs reassurance plus clear warning signs.
notes: Source was a bare vocabulary question (name of postpartum discharge), tautological as a key; re-angled to a reassure-versus-investigate decision using the same learning point. Live items (OG050, DS020, PAOG032, PAQ16482, PAQ16356) all test abnormal bleeding or infection, not normal lochia. No figures keyed.

stem:
A 31-year-old teaching assistant who is 14 weeks pregnant spent an hour in a small classroom with a pupil who was sent home because of a blistering rash that the school nurse thinks is chickenpox. She cannot remember whether she had chickenpox as a child and has never been vaccinated. She feels well and has no rash herself.

What is the most appropriate first step?

options.A: Check her immune status and seek urgent specialist advice
options.B: Give a live varicella vaccine today to protect her and the baby
options.C: Reassure her that no action is needed unless a rash appears
options.D: Prescribe an oral antibiotic to prevent bacterial superinfection
options.E: Offer counselling about termination because of the exposure

correct_answer: A. Check her immune status and seek urgent specialist advice
why_correct: A pregnant woman with significant contact and no reliable history of chickenpox needs her immunity established urgently, usually with a varicella-zoster IgG test, together with prompt specialist advice. If she is non-immune she can be offered post-exposure prophylaxis, an antiviral or varicella-zoster immunoglobulin, because chickenpox in pregnancy carries risks for both mother and fetus. Source: NICE CKS, Chickenpox: Scenario: Exposure to chickenpox, Last revised in November 2023.
why_wrong: B. Live vaccines are not given in pregnancy and a vaccine would not protect her in time after exposure. C. Waiting for a rash wastes the window in which prophylaxis can be given. D. Antibiotics have no role in preventing chickenpox. E. Exposure alone is not an indication for termination, and she may well be immune.
pearl: In pregnancy, significant chickenpox contact with unclear immunity means check varicella-zoster IgG and take urgent specialist advice, not wait and see.
thinking: Significant contact with probable chickenpox  ↓  Pregnant with uncertain chickenpox history  ↓  Establish immunity with varicella-zoster IgG  ↓  Urgent specialist advice on prophylaxis if non-immune
exam_trap: C, reassurance until a rash appears, tempts because she feels well, but prophylaxis must be given early and depends on knowing her immune status.
takeaway: Check immunity and seek specialist advice promptly after significant chickenpox contact in pregnancy.
notes: Same learning point as source (establish immunity, seek prompt advice) in a new school-contact vignette with live-vaccine, reassurance, antibiotic and termination distractors. Not a duplicate of live ID018 (IgG-negative woman, key is aciclovir prophylaxis) or PAAKT180/PAQ15264 (woman with a rash). Checked: CKS says seek urgent specialist advice and IgG testing may be done in primary care if results are available within 24-48 hours; the key does not depend on that window. Source item UN3337 treated as a within-batch repeat of this one.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman has a positive home pregnancy test and her last period was about five weeks ago. She has had light brown spotting since yesterday but has no abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain or dizziness and looks well. Two years ago she had a right tubal ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Advise her to repeat the urine pregnancy test in about a week and return if bleeding continues
options.B: Reassure her and book routine antenatal care with the community midwife
options.C: Refer her to the early pregnancy assessment service because of her ectopic history
options.D: Prescribe a single dose of methotrexate in case the pregnancy is tubal
options.E: Start progesterone pessaries to reduce the chance of miscarriage

correct_answer: C. Refer her to the early pregnancy assessment service because of her ectopic history
why_correct: A previous ectopic pregnancy is a recognised risk factor for another, so this woman should have the pregnancy located by early assessment and ultrasound rather than being managed expectantly as a low-risk woman with early bleeding would be. Early pregnancy assessment services accept self-referral from women with a previous ectopic pregnancy. About a third of ectopic pregnancies occur in women with no risk factors, so the possibility must always be considered. Source: NICE NG126, Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management, 2019 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Watchful waiting with a repeat test is only for women with early bleeding and no risk factors such as a previous ectopic pregnancy. B. Routine booking would leave the pregnancy location unconfirmed and a possible ectopic pregnancy undiagnosed. D. Methotrexate is given only once an ectopic pregnancy has been confirmed. E. Progesterone does not address the main concern, which is excluding an ectopic pregnancy, and is not given before the pregnancy has been located.
pearl: A previous ectopic pregnancy raises the chance of another, so a new positive test with bleeding should prompt early assessment to locate the pregnancy.
thinking: Positive test with early spotting  ↓  Previous tubal ectopic pregnancy is a risk factor  ↓  Low-risk watchful waiting does not apply  ↓  Refer to the early pregnancy assessment service
exam_trap: A, repeat the urine test and wait, tempts because she is well and has no pain, but that advice is reserved for women without risk factors such as a previous ectopic pregnancy.
takeaway: Previous ectopic pregnancy means early scan and assessment in any new pregnancy.
notes: Source item was a recall of 'previous ectopic increases recurrence risk'; re-angled to the management decision that follows from the risk factor (NG126 rec 1.4.10 limits expectant management to women without risk factors such as previous ectopic; rec 1.3.3 self-referral). The stem gives 'about five weeks' only as scenario context; the key does not depend on a gestation threshold. No live item on this point (live ectopic items PAOG005, PAOG013, PAQ928, OG040, OG043 are diagnosis or treatment).

stem:
A 44-year-old woman has had light bleeding after sex on and off for three months, with occasional spotting between periods. Her last cervical screening result was normal. On speculum examination a soft, smooth, red, finger-like growth on a narrow stalk is seen emerging from the cervical canal. The rest of the cervix looks healthy and the uterus is normal in size on bimanual examination.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Cervical ectropion with friable epithelium
options.B: Nabothian cyst of the cervix
options.C: Early invasive cervical cancer
options.D: Benign cervical polyp
options.E: Prolapsed submucosal fibroid

correct_answer: D. Benign cervical polyp
why_correct: A soft, smooth, red, finger-like growth arising from the endocervical canal is the typical appearance of a cervical polyp, a common benign cause of postcoital and intermenstrual bleeding. Polyps are usually removed in clinic and sent for histology. A cervix that looks consistent with cancer, which is not the case here, would need a suspected cancer pathway referral. Source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Ectropion is a flat red area of glandular epithelium around the os, not a growth projecting from the canal. B. Nabothian cysts are smooth, pale or yellowish retention cysts on the cervical surface and do not usually bleed. C. Cervical cancer typically gives an irregular, friable or ulcerated cervix rather than a smooth stalked growth on an otherwise healthy cervix. E. A prolapsed fibroid is usually larger and broader and is accompanied by an enlarged uterus.
pearl: A smooth stalked growth from the cervical os with bleeding after sex is a cervical polyp, but any cervix that looks suspicious still needs suspected cancer pathway referral.
thinking: Bleeding after sex and between periods  ↓  Visible smooth red stalked growth from the os  ↓  Rest of the cervix and uterus look normal  ↓  Cervical polyp
exam_trap: A, cervical ectropion, also causes bleeding after sex and tempts, but it is a flat red area on the cervical surface rather than a growth projecting from the canal.
takeaway: A smooth, soft, stalked growth from the os is a cervical polyp, a benign cause of postcoital bleeding.
notes: Source stem was a one-line recall item; built a speculum-finding vignette with ectropion, Nabothian cyst, cancer and prolapsed fibroid as distractors. Key checked against standard gynaecology teaching: no NHS/CKS page for cervical polyps was reachable (nhs.uk, patient.info, nhsinform URLs returned 404 or no content), so NICE NG12 rec 1.5.16 was opened only to support the point that a cancer-looking cervix needs suspected cancer pathway referral. Reviewer may wish to add an RCOG or BSCCP source. No live cervical polyp item found in the bank (live OG025, DF092, PAOG065, PAQ921 cover other postcoital bleeding points).

stem:
A 27-year-old woman who is 18 weeks pregnant has had two days of stinging when she passes urine and needing to go more often. She has no fever, loin pain or vomiting, her observations are normal, and she has no drug allergies. A urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leucocytes.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Advise increased fluids and offer a back-up antibiotic prescription to use if symptoms persist
options.B: Send a midstream urine culture and start an antibiotic suitable in pregnancy now
options.C: Withhold antibiotics until the culture result is available, then treat
options.D: Prescribe antibiotics only if she develops a fever or loin pain
options.E: Advise cranberry juice and repeat the dipstick at her next antenatal visit

correct_answer: B. Send a midstream urine culture and start an antibiotic suitable in pregnancy now
why_correct: A pregnant woman with symptoms of a lower urinary tract infection should be offered an immediate antibiotic, with a midstream urine sample sent for culture before the first dose. Untreated infection can ascend to the kidneys and is associated with premature birth. The antibiotic is reviewed against the culture result, and nitrofurantoin, a usual first choice, is avoided at term. Source: NICE NG109, Urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Back-up prescriptions and delayed treatment are for non-pregnant women, not for pregnancy. C. Waiting for the culture delays treatment in a woman at higher risk of complications. D. Waiting for a fever or loin pain means treating only once the infection may already have reached the kidneys. E. Cranberry juice and re-testing later do not treat an established infection.
pearl: Lower urinary tract infection in pregnancy is treated at once, after sending a urine culture, because of the risk of pyelonephritis and premature birth.
thinking: Dysuria and frequency with positive dipstick  ↓  Pregnant, so higher risk of ascending infection  ↓  Immediate antibiotic plus midstream urine culture  ↓  Review choice against sensitivities
exam_trap: A, a back-up prescription, tempts because it is standard for uncomplicated infection in non-pregnant women, but NICE advises immediate treatment in pregnancy.
takeaway: In pregnancy, treat symptomatic lower UTI immediately and send a urine culture.
notes: Source item was a 'why is prompt assessment important' reasoning question with a weak key; re-angled to a management decision testing the same principle (prompt treatment because of ascending infection and pregnancy complications). Key checked against NG109 recs 1.1.5-1.1.7 and table 2 (page shows no update date, published 31 October 2018). No live lower-UTI-in-pregnancy item found (live DS145 is pyelonephritis in pregnancy, a different decision).

stem:
A 27-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome (PMOS), diagnosed three years ago, attends for review. She has irregular periods and central weight gain, and her BMI is in the obese range. Dark, velvety skin is noted at the back of her neck. She asks what she should be watching out for in her long-term health.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: She is mainly at risk of early menopause, so should have regular bone-density scans and hormone testing
options.B: She is at increased risk of type 2 diabetes, so advise lifestyle change and glucose checks
options.C: She is at risk of type 1 diabetes, so islet autoantibody testing should be arranged now
options.D: She has a high ovarian cancer risk, so should have regular CA-125 and pelvic scanning
options.E: Her long-term risks are no higher than average, so no monitoring is needed after diagnosis

correct_answer: B. She is at increased risk of type 2 diabetes, so advise lifestyle change and glucose checks
why_correct: PMOS (formerly PCOS) is associated with insulin resistance, which is worsened by excess weight, and carries a long-term risk of impaired glucose tolerance, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Women should be told about these risks, encouraged to adopt healthy lifestyle measures with weight management where appropriate, and have their metabolic risk reviewed periodically. Source: NICE CKS, Polycystic ovary syndrome, Last revised in March 2025.
why_wrong: A. PMOS is not a cause of early menopause, and bone density is not routinely monitored. C. Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune and is not linked to insulin resistance in PMOS. D. Ovarian cancer risk is not raised enough to justify CA-125 screening, although endometrial cancer risk is increased with prolonged amenorrhoea. E. Long-term metabolic and cardiovascular risks are higher than average, so follow-up is needed.
pearl: PMOS raises the long-term risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, so counsel and review accordingly.
thinking: PMOS with obesity and acanthosis nigricans  ↓  Insulin resistance is the driver  ↓  Long-term type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk  ↓  Lifestyle and weight advice with periodic glucose review  ↓  Counsel on type 2 diabetes risk and check glucose periodically
exam_trap: C, type 1 diabetes, tempts because both are diabetes, but PMOS acts through insulin resistance, which leads to type 2 disease.
takeaway: Counsel women with PMOS about type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk and review them periodically.
notes: Re-angled from a recall item (which condition) to an advice/monitoring decision. No testing interval or numeric threshold keyed. Live PMOS items (END033, OG030, DS141, DS142) cover diagnosis and amenorrhoea, not long-term metabolic risk. CKS summary, complications and management-adults pages opened; all show Last revised in March 2025. The CA-125 and early-menopause distractor rebuttals are standard teaching, not read from CKS.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman who is in the second trimester of her first pregnancy attends her antenatal appointment in October. She is otherwise well and has no long-term conditions. The midwife offers the seasonal flu vaccine, but she says a friend warned her that the injection could give her flu and harm the baby, so she would rather wait until after the birth.

Which is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Wait until the third trimester, because earlier vaccination is not considered safe for the baby
options.B: Have the vaccine only if she develops a long-term health condition during the pregnancy
options.C: Have the inactivated vaccine now, as it protects her and gives her baby early protection
options.D: Avoid all vaccines until after delivery, because vaccination in pregnancy is unsafe
options.E: Have the live nasal spray instead, because it is gentler on the developing baby

correct_answer: C. Have the inactivated vaccine now, as it protects her and gives her baby early protection
why_correct: The injected flu vaccine used in the UK contains no live virus, so it cannot cause flu, and it is safe at any stage of pregnancy. Pregnancy raises the risk of serious complications from flu, and vaccination also protects the baby during the first months of life. Pregnant women are therefore offered it each season. Source: NHS.uk, Flu vaccine in pregnancy and who can have the flu vaccine, 2026 to 2027 season.
why_wrong: A. It is safe in any trimester, so waiting for the third trimester leaves her unprotected for longer. B. Pregnancy itself is an eligibility reason, so no other condition is needed. D. Inactivated flu vaccine is recommended in pregnancy, and not all vaccines are avoided. E. The nasal spray contains live attenuated virus and is not used in pregnancy.
pearl: Pregnant women are offered inactivated flu vaccine at any stage of pregnancy, which also protects the newborn.
thinking: Pregnant woman declining flu vaccine over safety fears  ↓  Injected vaccine has no live virus  ↓  Pregnancy raises complication risk from flu  ↓  Safe at any stage and protects the baby  ↓  Offer the inactivated vaccine now
exam_trap: E, the live nasal spray, tempts as a gentler option, but live vaccines are avoided in pregnancy and the injected vaccine is the one used.
takeaway: Seasonal flu vaccination is recommended in pregnancy, whatever the stage.
notes: Source key sound. Reworded so the key is not 'recommended in pregnancy' restated; stem has a safety-concern angle and a distractor (live nasal spray) that tests the live/inactivated distinction (the live-spray exclusion in pregnancy is standard UK teaching, not stated on the fetched NHS page). No live pregnancy-flu question found (searched pregnan* with vaccin/influenza/flu: only MMR/rubella items). NHS page says safe at any stage of pregnancy and cannot give flu. The Green Book chapter 19 page was opened but only the NHS page was relied on.

stem:
A 46-year-old woman has had six months of progressively heavier periods with spotting between them. Her pregnancy test is negative, her cervical screening is up to date and normal, and abdominal and pelvic examination are normal. She mentions she has been wondering whether this is the start of the menopause.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Prescribe tranexamic acid during menses and review her in three months
options.B: Start the combined oral contraceptive pill to regulate her cycle without further tests
options.C: Reassure her that this is typical of the perimenopause and review if it persists for six months
options.D: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system straight away without assessing the uterine cavity
options.E: Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy to assess the uterine cavity

correct_answer: E. Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy to assess the uterine cavity
why_correct: Persistent bleeding between periods alongside heavy periods suggests possible structural or endometrial pathology, such as a polyp, fibroid or hyperplasia, so the cause should be investigated rather than treated empirically. Hysteroscopy allows direct inspection of the uterine cavity and biopsy when needed. Source: NICE NG88, Heavy menstrual bleeding: assessment and management, 2018 (page last updated July 2026).
why_wrong: A. Tranexamic acid treats heavy bleeding but does not exclude a cavity abnormality causing the intermenstrual bleeding. B. Hormonal cycle control without investigation could mask structural or endometrial pathology. C. Attributing persistent intermenstrual bleeding to perimenopause delays diagnosis. D. A levonorgestrel intrauterine system is a first-line treatment for heavy bleeding but only after the cavity has been assessed when there are features of pathology.
pearl: Persistent intermenstrual bleeding with heavy periods warrants hysteroscopic assessment before empirical hormonal treatment.
thinking: 46-year-old with heavy periods and intermenstrual bleeding  ↓  Pregnancy excluded, cervix screened  ↓  Possible polyp, fibroid or endometrial pathology  ↓  Assess the cavity, not treat blindly  ↓  Outpatient hysteroscopy
exam_trap: D, inserting the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, tempts because it is first-line for heavy bleeding, but with persistent intermenstrual bleeding the cavity needs assessment first.
takeaway: New intermenstrual bleeding with heavy periods needs investigation, not empirical treatment or reassurance.
notes: Source key ('investigate') made concrete using NG88 1.3.4 (offer outpatient hysteroscopy if persistent intermenstrual bleeding or risk factors) and 1.3.10. No age cut-off, thickness measurement or day count keyed (the stem age and six months are context only). Live HMB items (BX463, DR104, PAQ894, PAQ16196) cover FBC, LNG-IUS for simple HMB and polyp diagnosis, not the investigate-first decision. NG88 page shows Last updated 07 July 2026; recommendations cited are marked [2007, amended 2018] and [2018], so the year cited is 2018.

stem:
A 26-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant attends her GP with two days of burning on passing urine and needing to pass urine more often than usual, with new lower abdominal discomfort. She is afebrile, with no loin pain or vomiting, and her blood pressure and pulse are normal. She says she thought the frequency was just part of being pregnant.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Reassure her that frequency is expected in pregnancy and review at her next routine antenatal visit
options.B: Send a midstream urine sample for culture and start an antibiotic suitable in pregnancy
options.C: Wait for the urine culture result before deciding whether any antibiotic is necessary
options.D: Arrange admission for intravenous antibiotics and an urgent renal tract ultrasound scan
options.E: Advise increased fluids and simple analgesia only, and withhold antibiotics unless fever develops

correct_answer: B. Send a midstream urine sample for culture and start an antibiotic suitable in pregnancy
why_correct: Dysuria with new symptoms in a pregnant woman suggests a lower urinary tract infection, which is treated with an immediate antibiotic because untreated infection can progress to pyelonephritis and is linked to preterm birth. A midstream urine sample is sent for culture before the first dose so that the antibiotic can be reviewed against the result, and the choice must be safe in pregnancy. Source: NICE NG109, Urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Frequency alone can be physiological, but burning and new discomfort are not, and delay risks pyelonephritis. C. Pregnant women with lower UTI should be given an immediate antibiotic, not left untreated while waiting for culture. D. She has no systemic features or loin pain, so oral treatment in the community is appropriate. E. Self-care alone is not enough in pregnancy, where antibiotic treatment is recommended.
pearl: In pregnancy, send a urine culture and treat lower UTI promptly with an antibiotic that is safe in pregnancy.
thinking: Pregnant with dysuria and new discomfort  ↓  Not just physiological frequency  ↓  No systemic features, so lower UTI  ↓  Culture before antibiotic, treat immediately  ↓  Urine culture and a pregnancy-safe antibiotic
exam_trap: A, reassurance that frequency is normal in pregnancy, tempts because frequency is common, but burning and discomfort signal infection.
takeaway: Treat symptomatic UTI in pregnancy promptly after sending urine for culture.
notes: Source key retained (treat promptly); added the culture step and the immediate-antibiotic angle per NG109 1.1.5 and 1.1.6. No drug names or durations keyed. The preterm-birth link is from NG109 1.2.1 (asymptomatic bacteriuria wording: risk factor for pyelonephritis and premature delivery). No live pregnancy-UTI question found (searched pregnan* with dysuria/urinary tract: only PAQ16102, pyelonephritis). NG109 page shows Published 31 October 2018; no later update date was visible.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman underwent egg collection for IVF five days ago after a long course of gonadotrophin injections, and an embryo was transferred. She now has increasing abdominal bloating and nausea, is passing much less urine than usual, and feels mildly breathless when lying flat. She is afebrile. The abdomen is distended and mildly tender with shifting dullness, and she has no localised guarding. Ultrasound shows both ovaries enlarged with free fluid in the abdomen, and her haematocrit is raised.

Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?

options.A: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
options.B: Torsion of an enlarged ovary
options.C: Heterotopic pregnancy with tubal rupture
options.D: Acute pelvic inflammatory disease after egg collection
options.E: Ovarian malignancy presenting with ascites

correct_answer: A. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
why_correct: Excessive ovarian response to stimulation causes enlarged ovaries and a shift of fluid out of the circulation, producing ascites, haemoconcentration, reduced urine output and breathlessness. The timing after stimulated treatment and the bilateral findings point to ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome rather than a surgical or infective cause. Mild cases settle with supportive care, but severe cases need admission for fluid balance and thromboprophylaxis. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 5, The Management of Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome, 2026 (page last reviewed April 2026).
why_wrong: B. Torsion causes sudden severe unilateral pain with vomiting, not bilateral enlargement with ascites and a rising haematocrit. C. Heterotopic pregnancy would give sharp unilateral pain and haemodynamic collapse from blood loss rather than haemoconcentration. D. Pelvic inflammatory disease would cause fever, discharge and cervical motion tenderness, with no fluid shift. E. Malignancy does not appear within days of ovarian stimulation and would not usually cause a raised haematocrit.
pearl: Think of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome whenever bloating, ascites and falling urine output follow fertility drug treatment.
thinking: Recent ovarian stimulation for IVF  ↓  Bloating, ascites, reduced urine output, breathlessness  ↓  Bilateral enlarged ovaries and raised haematocrit  ↓  Fluid shift from excess ovarian response  ↓  Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
exam_trap: B, torsion of an enlarged ovary, tempts because enlarged stimulated ovaries do twist, but torsion gives sudden one-sided pain rather than a bilateral picture with fluid shift.
takeaway: Abdominal distension with falling urine output after fertility treatment suggests ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.
notes: Re-angled from the bare recall item into a vignette with the discriminating features (haemoconcentration, ascites, oliguria). Source key (OHSS) confirmed sound. No live OHSS question in plab1-questions.js (searched OHSS / ovarian hyperstimulation). Key is the shortest option. The NHS IVF risks page also lists OHSS symptoms needing urgent care. RCOG page text confirms OHSS is a complication of stimulation, self-limiting in most, severe cases needing inpatient care; the thromboprophylaxis statement is standard teaching not read from the fetched summary page.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman at 35 weeks of pregnancy is brought to the maternity unit by ambulance after sudden constant severe abdominal pain with dark vaginal bleeding.
